newsitem.title: GERMANY: German unions to meet bosses to solve sick pay row.
newsitem.headline: German unions to meet bosses to solve sick pay row.

text.p: Talks between German engineering union IG Metall and employers' association Gesamtmetall are to take place on Monday to try to resolve a feud over planned cut-backs to sick pay, union officials said on Saturday.
If compromise on sick pay cannot be reached around the negotiating table, Germany will see "tougher strikes than the country has ever experienced", Walter Riester, vice-chairman of IG Metall, warned.

In an interview in Sunday's edition of the Berlin newspaper Tagesspiegel, released to the media in advance, Riester said meaningful negotiations could take place only if Gesamtmetall revised its postion.

Wildcat strike action has already hit production at many of Germany's largest car companies. IG Metall, representing some 3.5 million metal and electronics workers, has led protests against the new law so far.

There are fears that the current outbreak of unrest could soon spread to other sectors and the talks will be closely monitored by employers and employees in other sectors, which also come under the sick pay changes.
The changes in sick pay come into law as part of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's austerity package. Under the new law, workers will get only 80 percent of their full pay for the first six weeks of illness.
If they wish, employees can give up one of their 30 annual vacation days to compensate for each week of absence.

The cuts would make estimated savings of 12 billion marks ($7.8 billion) a year. However, to many union leaders the new legislation harks back to the old system before the much-cherished post-war economic miracle.

"This republic cannot return to the situation we had before 1956. If necessary, IG Metall will choose a strike in exactly the same way as they did in Schleswig-Holstein 40 years ago," Klaus Zwickel, chairman of IG Metall said last week.
This refers to an almost-legendary 114-day strike by metal workers in the northern state that established many of the conditions workers in Germany now take for granted.
Around 10,000 workers walked out at Daimler Benz AG's Mercedes plant in Stuttgart on Tuesday, while thousands of workers at General Motors Adam Opel and Ford's German unit protested on the same day.
Deutsche Bank AG said last Thursday that it had implemented the new sick-pay cuts, while Deutsche's rival Commerzbank AG previously said it was also planning to introduce the new scheme.
German banking sector unions have said that banks face warning strikes if the employers implement the sick pay law.
Zwickel and Riester will meet with Gesamtmetall president Werner Stumpfe and Dieter Hundt, the vice-president, at 1300 GMT in a hotel near Frankfurt.

Although employers and workers have discussed the planned cuts in individual factories and workplaces, the meeting will be the first time top representatives from both sides have met to tackle the sensitive issue.
